title: Penetrant Testing of Castings | MSS SP-93 PT (US)
description: Dye penetrant inspection of aluminum, stainless and steel castings to MSS SP-93, ASTM E165 and Section V, mobilized across the US. Request a PT quote.
h1: Penetrant Testing of Castings: Dye Penetrant Inspection to MSS SP-93
html:
Penetrant testing of castings finds cracks, hot tears, cold shuts, shrinkage and porosity that are open to the surface of aluminum, stainless, steel and nonferrous castings. Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to foundries, machine shops, receiving docks and plants across the United States to examine castings to MSS SP-93, ASTM E165 and E1417, and ASME Section V Article 6. Request a PT inspection quote with your casting drawings and specification.

What penetrant inspection of castings is for

A casting is made by pouring metal into a mold, and its flaws come from how the metal freezes. Liquid penetrant testing (PT) shows the ones that reach the surface. Foundry practice relies on it for nonferrous castings, stainless steel and other non-magnetic alloys, and for any casting where the buyer wants an independent surface check after machining, repair or heat treatment. Carbon and low-alloy steel castings are often examined with magnetic particles instead; where both are allowed, penetrant is used when the surface is non-magnetic or the specification names it.

The typical customers are manufacturers and operators that buy cast valve bodies, pump casings, flanges and fittings, turbine and compressor casings, engine and transmission housings, and structural brackets. Our crews examine incoming lots, finished machined castings, weld repairs and castings returned from service.

Casting flaws and what they look like

  • Porosity. Gas holes or microshrinkage that reach the surface show as scattered round or sponge-like clusters, often concentrated near thick sections.
  • Shrinkage. Cavities from the last metal to freeze. At the surface they appear as rough, branched or feathery indications at hot spots and section changes.
  • Hot tears. Jagged cracks that form while the casting is still weak, usually at junctions and corners.
  • Cold shuts and laps. Smooth, continuous lines where two streams of metal met without fusing.
  • Cracks from heat treatment or machining. Straight or crescent-shaped lines, often at stress risers.
  • Weld repair defects. Cracks and lack of fusion in the repair weld and its heat-affected zone.

Telling these apart is the main skill. A technician who reads indications by their shape, location, and bleed-out behavior can separate a crack from a pore, and a real indication from a machining burr or a rough as-cast background. Reference photographs, such as ASTM E433, are used to compare what appears on the part with accepted typical indications.

Codes and acceptance for castings

MSS SP-93 is the Manufacturers Standardization Society quality standard for liquid penetrant examination of steel castings and forgings for valves, flanges, fittings and other piping components. It describes the method, indication types and acceptance for those parts. For general practice we follow ASTM E165 for the penetrant examination and ASTM E1417 where fluorescent process control is specified. Code castings in pressure equipment, for example parts of a boiler or pressure vessel, follow ASME Section V Article 6 for the examination and the construction code for acceptance. Aerospace, automotive or customer-specific castings use the specification the purchaser names, and we apply it as written.

Acceptance criteria are not ours to choose. The drawing, the purchase order or the code decides whether an indication is acceptable, and your engineer or purchaser's inspector applies it. Written procedures are approved by an ASNT Level III, and technicians are qualified under SNT-TC-1A through the company's written practice.

For method background see the plain-language explanation of Article 6.

As-cast surfaces change the technique

A weld is smooth; a casting often is not. Sand casting leaves a rough, porous skin that traps penetrant and produces a heavy background. Investment castings are smoother but have their own surface features. Machined faces are cleaner and show crisp indications. This drives the system we choose:

  • Water-washable penetrant removes easily from rough surfaces and is common for as-cast and shop work, but is less able to hold in fine flaws and is more sensitive to over-washing.
  • Solvent-removable penetrant gives better control on machined faces and in the field, at a cost in cleaning time on rough surfaces.
  • Post-emulsifiable systems give high sensitivity on critical parts but need emulsifier control and a shop setup.
  • Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive than visible dye and is used where the specification requires it, with ultraviolet light in a darkened area.

The technician judges background on the actual surface. If a casting is too rough to read reliably, the report says so and the buyer decides whether to blast, machine or dress it before re-examination.

Surface preparation, impregnation and rework

Surface preparation is the step that decides the quality of the result. Sand and shot blasting peen the surface and can close a flaw; machining and grinding can smear metal across an opening. For that reason the procedure may call for chemical etching after mechanical cleaning on soft metals like aluminum, followed by a rinse and thorough drying. Parts are cleaned of oil, cutting fluid and paint, because they block penetrant entry.

Impregnation matters too. Resin impregnation is used on aluminum and other castings to seal leak paths, and once porosity is sealed, penetrant cannot enter it. Examination is therefore planned before impregnation, and after any repair. After grinding out a defect, the area is re-examined to confirm the flaw is gone, and after weld repair and heat treatment, the full surface is re-examined. Rework history is recorded in the report so the purchaser can see how many cycles a casting went through.

Technique, step by step

  1. Clean and prepare. Remove oils, coatings and loose scale; etch if the procedure requires it.
  2. Dry. Castings hold moisture in porosity; heat drying and a cool-down are part of the process.
  3. Apply penetrant and dwell. Dwell comes from the procedure and the alloy and flaw type.
  4. Remove excess. Water spray on water-washable systems at controlled pressure and temperature, or solvent wipe for solvent-removable systems.
  5. Develop. A thin coat of developer; indications bleed out and are read within the specified window.
  6. Interpret and record. Classify by type and size and compare with the acceptance standard.
  7. Post-clean parts, especially before machining, coating or assembly.

The standard temperature range for the process in Article 6 is 40 to 125 °F (5 to 52 °C). Foundry floors and heat-treat areas can fall outside this range, so the procedure is qualified for the actual temperature or the part is brought into range.

Materials and where they show up

Aluminum castings appear in automotive and industrial components; see our automotive penetrant testing page. Aircraft ground-support and tooling castings are covered under aviation penetrant work, where the customer's specification governs and Atlantis does not sign off airworthiness. Stainless valve and pump castings in chemical plants and hygienic plants need low-halogen materials and cleaning, covered on the stainless steel penetrant page. Turbine, valve and pump castings in power generation are examined during outages and receiving.

Receiving inspection and sampling

Many buyers use penetrant at the dock rather than in the foundry. A lot of valve bodies or pump casings arrives, a sample is drawn according to the purchase order or the plan in the specification, and the sample is examined on the machined and unmachined faces that the drawing calls out. A rejection in the sample can trigger examination of the whole lot, so we record lot and heat numbers and the sampling plan in the report. Machined sealing faces, bores, flange faces and thread roots get particular attention because a flaw there is a leak path.

Planning realities for casting work

Technicians are mobilized to your site for an agreed scope. Casting inspection is a production activity, so a clean, dry, well-lit, ventilated bench or booth, drain for water-washable systems, and a way to dry parts make the work faster. Fluorescent work needs a darkened area. Heavy castings need lifting and turning equipment from your side. On outdoor yards, weather and temperature limits apply. Material safety data sheets for penetrants are supplied before we arrive, and flammable solvents follow your site rules.

What the report contains

Each report lists the part number and drawing revision, heat or lot number, material and condition, the specification and acceptance level, the procedure and revision, penetrant system and lot numbers, surface condition and preparation, temperature, dwell and developer times, the technician and level, indications recorded by location and size on a sketch or photograph, and accept or reject. If a casting is rejected, the reason is stated against the specification. An ASNT Level III reviews the report, and we leave the disposition, repair and remaining-life questions to your engineer.

What to send for a quote

  • Drawings, part numbers and quantities of castings.
  • Alloy and casting process: sand, investment, die, permanent mold.
  • Specification, such as MSS SP-93, a customer standard or a code, and the acceptance level.
  • Surface condition: as-cast, blasted, machined, impregnated.
  • Where the examination will be done: foundry, shop, receiving dock or plant.
  • Site address, access, permits and schedule constraints.

Where we work in the United States

  • Detroit for automotive and heavy-equipment castings in Michigan.
  • Milwaukee for foundries and machining shops across Wisconsin.
  • Cleveland for iron, steel and aluminum casting plants in northern Ohio.
  • Wichita for aluminum and nonferrous castings supporting aircraft work in Kansas.
  • Grand Rapids for foundry and tooling shops in western Michigan.
  • Birmingham for iron-casting and pipe-fitting foundries in Alabama.
  • Houston for valve and pump castings used in energy plants.
  • Indianapolis for powertrain and industrial castings in Indiana.

Train your own technicians

Foundries and machine shops that want their own technicians can use PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training together with the penetrant testing simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A, your employer certifies its own personnel.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, so internal casting soundness is not examined by us with that method, and we do not offer specialist techniques on this page. We do not release castings, decide rework or approve parts for service. The penetrant testing overview covers the method in general.

faq.a: MSS SP-93 is the Manufacturers Standardization Society quality standard for liquid penetrant examination of steel castings and forgings used for valves, flanges, fittings and other piping components. It covers the method, indication types and acceptance, and the purchase order or code says whether it applies.

faq.q: Can you examine aluminum castings with dye penetrant?
faq.a: Yes. Aluminum is non-magnetic, so penetrant is the standard surface method. Surface preparation is more delicate because aluminum smears under grinding and blasting, so etching may be specified. We also plan the examination before any impregnation that would seal porosity.

faq.q: How do you tell porosity from a crack?
faq.a: By shape and behavior. Porosity shows as round or clustered indications that bleed out slowly, while a crack shows as a continuous, often jagged line. Location, orientation and a repeat examination after wiping help. Reference photographs such as ASTM E433 support the comparison.

faq.q: Why is penetrant testing harder on as-cast surfaces?
faq.a: Sand-cast skins are rough and porous, so penetrant stays in the texture and creates a heavy background that can hide real indications. Water-washable systems and controlled removal help, and if the surface is unreadable, the report says so and the buyer decides whether to dress it.

faq.q: Should penetrant testing be done before or after machining?
faq.a: Both can be needed. Examination after machining shows flaws exposed by metal removal and checks sealing faces. Because machining can smear metal, surface preparation or etching is specified. Impregnation should come after examination, because sealed porosity cannot be seen by penetrant.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to casting PT?
faq.a: The Article 6 standard range is roughly 40 to 125 °F. Foundry floors and heat-treat areas may fall outside it, so the procedure is qualified at the actual temperature or the part is allowed to come into range first.

faq.q: Can you check ferrous castings with penetrant instead of magnetic particle?
faq.a: Carbon and low-alloy steel castings can be examined with either method, and the specification usually names one. Magnetic particle is often faster on ferrous parts; penetrant is used on non-magnetic alloys or when the purchase order requires it. We follow the order.

faq.q: Who decides if a casting is acceptable?
faq.a: The drawing, purchase order or code sets the acceptance level, and your engineer or the purchaser's inspector applies it. Our Level II technician records and classifies indications, an ASNT Level III reviews the report, and we leave the decision on rework or release to you.

faq.q: What do you need to quote casting PT?
faq.a: Send drawings, quantities, alloy and process, the specification and acceptance level, surface condition, location of the work, access and the site address. If castings are going to be impregnated or machined, tell us the sequence so the examination is scheduled before sealing.
